Detailed entries for `QPKG-012..QPKG-020`. Each follows the four-part
**What / Why / How / When NOT to apply** shape. The service script is the file
named by `QPKG_SERVICE_PROGRAM`; QTS links it as `/etc/init.d/<script>` and
runs it as root at boot, shutdown, and on every App Center start, stop and
restart. The QDK template is `shared/init.sh` in
[qnap-dev/QDK](https://github.com/qnap-dev/QDK).

---

## QPKG-012 — Guard `start`, and only `start`, with the `Enable` check

**What.** The `start` branch reads the package's `Enable` field from
`/etc/config/qpkg.conf` exactly as the QDK template does and exits when it is
not `TRUE`. No other branch checks it.

**Why.** At boot QTS runs `start` for every installed package. Without the
guard, a package the user disabled in App Center starts again after the next
reboot (QDK guide Cookbook, "A disabled service is restarted at reboot").
Putting the same check on `stop` breaks stopping, because QTS sets `Enable`
to `FALSE` before it calls `stop`.

**How.**

```sh
CONF=/etc/config/qpkg.conf
QPKG_NAME=myapp
case "$1" in
  start)
    ENABLED=$(/sbin/getcfg "$QPKG_NAME" Enable -u -d FALSE -f "$CONF")
    if [ "$ENABLED" != "TRUE" ]; then
        echo "$QPKG_NAME is disabled."
        exit 1
    fi
    do_start
    ;;
  stop) do_stop ;;
esac
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never. Even a package that only links files must
respect the user's disable.

## QPKG-013 — Implement `start`, `stop`, `restart` and `remove`

**What.** The service script handles `start`, `stop`, `restart` and
`remove`, prints usage and exits non-zero for anything else. `restart` is
`stop` followed by `start`. `remove` undoes what `start` set up outside the
package directory.

**Why.** The generated `.uninstall.sh` runs `<script> stop`, then
`<script> remove`, then waits 5 s before deleting the package directory
(`qinstall.sh`). A script without `remove` leaves its out-of-tree state
behind on uninstall (QPKG-026).

**How.**

```sh
  restart) "$0" stop; "$0" start ;;
  remove)  rm -f /usr/bin/myapp ;;
  *) echo "Usage: $0 {start|stop|restart|remove}"; exit 1 ;;
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never. `status` is a useful addition, not a
replacement.

---

## QPKG-014 — Resolve the install dir at runtime with `getcfg`

**What.** The service script and every runtime helper find the package
directory with `getcfg <name> Install_Path` and stop when it is missing. No
script hard-codes `/share/CACHEDEV1_DATA/.qpkg/...`.

**Why.** The package lives at `<volume>/.qpkg/<name>` on whichever volume the
user picked (QPKG-029), and users can migrate it to another volume later.
A hard-coded path works on the developer's NAS and fails, or writes to the
wrong volume, everywhere else (QDK guide §7).

**How.**

```sh
QPKG_ROOT=$(/sbin/getcfg "$QPKG_NAME" Install_Path -d "" -f /etc/config/qpkg.conf)
[ -d "$QPKG_ROOT" ] || { echo "$QPKG_NAME: install path missing"; exit 1; }
```

**When NOT to apply.** Inside `package_routines` hooks, use `$SYS_QPKG_DIR`,
which the installer sets.

---

## QPKG-015 — Recreate out-of-tree state on every `start`; remove it on `stop`

**What.** Anything a package puts outside its `.qpkg` directory — symlinks in
`/usr/bin` or `/opt`, web-server include files, files in `/etc` — is created
by `start` and removed by `stop`. Nothing outside the package directory is
written once at install time and expected to persist.

**Why.** The QTS root filesystem is a RAM disk rebuilt at boot; QNAP says
default config files "are reset on every startup"
([Running your own application at startup](https://www.qnap.com/en/how-to/faq/article/running-your-own-application-at-startup),
2023-07-06). A symlink made only in `pkg_post_install` exists until the first
reboot. QNAP's QuObjects service script follows this pattern: `start` relinks
its web UI into the QTS web server's `cgi-bin/qpkg/` directory and recreates
`/var/run/swift`.

**How.**

```sh
do_start() {
    ln -sf "$QPKG_ROOT/bin/myapp" /usr/bin/myapp
    cp "$QPKG_ROOT/etc/apache-myapp.conf" /etc/default_config/apache/extra/
    ...
}
do_stop() {
    ...
    rm -f /usr/bin/myapp /etc/default_config/apache/extra/apache-myapp.conf
}
```

**When NOT to apply.** Files under `/etc/config/` persist across reboots by
design; manage those with `setcfg` and clean them up on uninstall
(QPKG-026).

## QPKG-016 — `start` returns success only after the service answers

**What.** `start` launches the daemon, records its PID, then polls the
process and its port or health endpoint until it answers or a bounded timeout
passes. It exits non-zero on timeout. It never ends in a bare background `&`
and reports success. `QPKG_TIMEOUT` covers the wait.

**Why.** App Center shows a package as running when `start` exits 0. A start
that backgrounds the daemon and returns reports success even when the daemon
dies a second later on a bad config or a busy port, and the user sees a
"running" package that serves nothing. QNAP's own QuObjects starts its Swift
servers with `swift.sh start &`. App Center service actions also have a
default timeout (OneCD's
[IncreaseTimeouts](https://github.com/OneCDOnly/IncreaseTimeouts) raises it),
so the wait must be bounded.

**How.**

```sh
# qpkg.cfg: QPKG_TIMEOUT="120,60"   (start,stop seconds)
"$QPKG_ROOT/bin/myapp" --config "$QPKG_ROOT/etc/myapp.conf" >>"$LOG" 2>&1 &
echo $! > "/var/run/$QPKG_NAME.pid"
i=0
until curl --silent --fail --max-time 1 "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health" >/dev/null; do
    kill -0 "$(cat "/var/run/$QPKG_NAME.pid")" 2>/dev/null || { echo "$QPKG_NAME died"; exit 1; }
    i=$((i + 1)); [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && { echo "$QPKG_NAME: no answer in 90 s"; exit 1; }
    sleep 1
done
```

**When NOT to apply.** A package with no long-running process (a CLI tool,
a set of symlinks) has nothing to poll.

## QPKG-017 — A `start` that finds a component running still starts the rest

**What.** Starting is idempotent per component: a helper that finds its
daemon already running returns, it does not `exit`. `start` then goes on to
the remaining components.

**Why.** `exit` inside a shell function ends the whole script. QuObjects'
`start_oss_daemon` runs `pidof oss-daemon && exit 0`, so when that daemon
survived a partial stop, `start` exits successfully without starting the
account updater, the scanner or Swift. App Center shows the package running
while its S3 endpoint is down.

**How.**

```sh
start_api() {
    pidof myapp-api >/dev/null && return 0
    "$QPKG_ROOT/bin/myapp-api" &
}
do_start() { start_api && start_worker && start_web; }
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never. Use `exit` only in the top-level `case`.

## QPKG-018 — Declare dependencies with `Dependency=` and wait for them

**What.** A package that needs another QPKG declares it in its `qpkg.conf`
entry with `Dependency=` (colon-separated), set in `pkg_post_install`. `start`
also waits, with a bounded retry, for the paths and services it needs. Do not
rely on `QPKG_RC_NUM` for ordering.

**Why.** After a reboot QTS ignores `QPKG_RC_NUM` and renumbers packages by
their order in `qpkg.conf`, starting at 100 (QDK guide §5). Since QTS 5.2.0
packages start asynchronously, so ordering tools stopped working
([OneCD, 2025-04-26](https://community.qnap.com/t/qpkg-sortmyqpkgs/1095)). A
package that assumes its dependency is already up fails at boot and works
after a manual restart.

**How.**

```sh
# package_routines
pkg_post_install() {
    $CMD_SETCFG "$QPKG_NAME" Dependency "Entware" -f "$SYS_QPKG_CONFIG_FILE"
}
# service script, inside do_start
i=0
until [ -x /opt/bin/opkg ]; do
    i=$((i + 1)); [ "$i" -ge 60 ] && { echo "Entware not ready"; exit 1; }
    sleep 1
done
```

**When NOT to apply.** A self-contained package with no dependency on another
QPKG or on a share being mounted.

---

## QPKG-019 — Export `QNAP_QPKG` in the service script

**What.** The service script exports `QNAP_QPKG=<name>` before it starts
anything.

**Why.** QTS Resource Monitor uses it to attribute child processes to the
package (QNAP "QPKG Development Guidelines", history 2.2.15). Without it, the
package's CPU and memory show up as unattributed system processes.

**How.**

```sh
export QNAP_QPKG=$QPKG_NAME
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never. It is one line in the QDK template.

---

## QPKG-020 — Keep the PID file in `/var/run` and logs on a data volume

**What.** The PID file goes in `/var/run/<name>.pid`. Logs go under the
package or data directory on a volume, with a size cap or rotation the
package implements itself.

**Why.** `/var/run` is cleared at boot, so a stale PID never survives a
reboot. The root filesystem is a small RAM disk (QPKG-015): logs written
under `/var/log` or `/tmp` vanish at reboot, when you need them most, and an
unbounded log there can fill RAM. No built-in QTS rotation for QPKG logs is
documented, so an uncapped log on a volume grows forever.

**How.**

```sh
PIDFILE=/var/run/$QPKG_NAME.pid
LOG=$QPKG_ROOT/log/$QPKG_NAME.log
mkdir -p "$QPKG_ROOT/log"
[ -f "$LOG" ] && [ "$(wc -c < "$LOG")" -gt 10485760 ] && mv "$LOG" "$LOG.1"
```

**When NOT to apply.** A daemon with its own rotating log writer only needs
the directory.
